_comment: Corrections applied to the vendored Copenhagen Alliance versification maps.
Every entry records what was wrong and how the fix was verified. These are not
preferences: each one is an upstream data error that would otherwise produce a
silently wrong citation. Re-check this file whenever the vendored maps are
refreshed -- the loader will complain if a correction no longer applies, which is
the signal that upstream fixed it and the entry can be dropped.
_psalm_9_note: The 'PSA 9:22 -> PSA 10:0' drop below is repeated for lxx, vul, rsc and rso -- every system that follows the Greek psalm numbering. Reason, once: the Septuagint merges Hebrew Psalms 9 and 10 into a single Psalm 9, so Greek 9:22-39 is Hebrew 10:1-18, which the neighbouring range entry already states exactly (39-22+1 = 18 = 18-1+1). The extra entry additionally sends Greek 9:22 to Hebrew 10:0, the superscription slot, which would make one Greek verse both the title and the first verse of the Hebrew psalm. Hebrew Psalm 10 has no superscription at all -- it is one of the few untitled psalms in Book I, which is part of why it is read as a continuation of Psalm 9 -- so verse 0 does not exist there to map onto.
_synodal_psalm_note: The rsc and rso files carry the Greek psalm numbering, as lxx and vul do, but state it in fragments rather than in whole ranges -- and several of those fragments contradict each other or map an unequal number of verses. lxx and vul each render the affected psalms as a single clean range ('PSA 86:0-7 -> PSA 87:0-7', 'PSA 89:0-17 -> PSA 90:0-17', 'PSA 141:0-8 -> PSA 142:0-8'), and every correction below reassembles exactly that alignment out of the pieces, keeping whichever fragments are already exact. Nothing here is an invention: the target is independently attested twice over, by two systems that load and are in daily use. Note that mappings onto verse 0 are *not* faults -- org has no verse 0 in the Psalms, but lxx and vul target it 139 and 149 times respectively, because it is how the Copenhagen data models the superscription slot. Only contradictions and unequal ranges block a load.
_dag_note: org has no DAG book at all -- Greek Daniel lives there as DAN plus the three standalone books S3Y, SUS and BEL. lxx.json spells the whole correspondence out; eng.json recorded only Susanna and Bel, so every English citation of Greek Daniel 1-12 fell through to 'org DAG x:y', a book the pivot does not have. The gap invariant in tests/test_alignment.py does not catch it because it skips books the target system lacks rather than refusing them, so this was silent. The ranges below mirror lxx's, which are verified, and differ only where the English tradition does: it keeps the Aramaic chapter break by printing 'Darius the Mede received the kingdom' as 5:31, where the Greek opens chapter 6 with it. Hence eng DAG 5 has 31 verses to the Greek's 30, eng DAG 6 has 28 to the Greek's 29, and everything in chapter 6 runs one behind. Measured on web against brenton: chapters 1-4 and 7-12 align verse for verse at offset 0, chapter 5 puts exactly one verse at the next chapter's opening, and all 28 verses of chapter 6 sit at +1.
_psalm_title_note: Examined and deliberately not corrected. lxx maps 135 of its 138 titled psalms as a single straight range from verse 0 -- 'PSA 12:0-6 -> PSA 13:0-6' -- while vul curates a handful of the same psalms by hand, and comparing the two suggests lxx is one out. It is not, or not in a way this file can fix. The Copenhagen data models a superscription as verse 0 on both sides of a mapping, while org's own maxVerses counts it as verse 1: the Leningrad Codex's Psalm 13:1 is 'lamnatzeach mizmor ledavid', the title, and org gives the psalm six verses. Those two conventions disagree upstream, so a mapping that looks off by one against the verse counts is consistent with the convention the mappings themselves use. Where vul departs from the straight range it is for a real reason and those entries stand: the Latin merges Psalm 12's title with its first line into one verse and splits the Hebrew's 13:3 in two, which is why it needs 12:2 and 12:3 both mapping to 13:3. Rewriting 135 lxx psalms on a convention this project does not control would risk far more than it fixes, and the measured cost of leaving them is seven flagged rows across the whole derivation. See audit.faithful_chapters, which cannot see this either.

eng.reason: Sends the standalone Song of the Three into book DAG, Greek Daniel -- which org does not have at all, so every one of these lands on a reference that cannot exist and org's own S3Y becomes unreachable from English. It is the same chain org.json carries (see ignore_self_mapped) and shares its faults: DAG 3:52 is claimed by both 'S3Y 1:1-29' and 'S3Y 1:30-31', and the final range cites S3Y verse 68 where org gives the book 67 verses. Dropped so English S3Y lines up with org's S3Y directly; the Song's position inside Greek Daniel is still reachable through the lxx and vul mappings, which state it cleanly as DAG 3:24-90.

Maps the English Letter of Jeremiah straight onto org's, verse for verse, and its last verse lands on LJE 1:73 -- which org does not have, since org gives the book 72. That ghost target is the same mechanical impossibility that identified the Jonah fault, in the opposite direction. The cause is the letter's heading: the English tradition counts 'A copy of a letter that Jeremy sent to those who were to be led captives into Babylon' as verse 1, and the Latin does not, so the English runs one ahead for the whole book. The Douay-Rheims opens Baruch 6 at 'For the sins that you have committed before God', which the World English Bible numbers 6:2, and the two agree again at the end -- 'Better therefore is the just man that hath no idols' is the Douay's 6:72 and the World English Bible's 6:73. Measured across the letter, English 6:n matches the Douay's 6:n-1 on 61 verses against 8 the other way. Replaced below by the shifted range.

lxx.reason: See _psalm_9_note. PSA 113:9 is the same artifact at the Psalm 114/115 split: Greek 113:9-26 is Hebrew 115:1-18 (26-9+1 = 18), and Hebrew Psalm 115 has no superscription for 113:9 to map onto.

Upstream lxx.json carries two contradictory layers of Greek Daniel mappings. The earlier layer ('DAG 4:1-3 -> DAN 3:31-33', 'DAG 4:4-37 -> DAN 4:1-34', 'DAG 5:1-30 -> DAN 5:1-30', 'DAG 6:1-29 -> DAN 6:1-29') is correct: Greek Daniel folds Hebrew 3:31-33 into chapter 4, which is the same offset eng.json records as 'DAN 4:1-3 -> DAN 3:31-33'. These three later entries contradict it and are provably wrong on their own terms -- 'DAG 5:1-31' cites a verse 31 that lxx's own maxVerses denies (Greek Daniel 5 has 30 verses), and 'DAG 6:1-28' is a truncation of the 29-verse chapter the same file maps correctly one line earlier.

vul.reason: See _psalm_9_note. PSA 113:9 is the same artifact one psalm-split later: the Septuagint's Psalm 113 is Hebrew 114 plus 115, so Greek 113:9-26 is Hebrew 115:1-18 (26-9+1 = 18), which the neighbouring range states exactly. The stray entry additionally sends Greek 113:9 to Hebrew 115:0, a superscription Psalm 115 does not have.

Contradicts the four hand-curated entries around it, which align the Vulgate's Psalm 12 to the Hebrew's Psalm 13 correctly: Hebrew Psalm 13 counts its superscription as verse 1, so the Latin's first line of text (12:1) is Hebrew 13:2, exactly as 'PSA 12:1 -> PSA 13:2' says. This range instead sends 12:1 to 13:1, putting the first line of the psalm on the superscription. Replaced below by a title-to-title mapping so the superscription stays reachable.

Contradicts 'SNG 1:1-16 -> SNG 1:2-17', which is exact and complete: the Vulgate's Song of Songs chapter 1 has 16 verses and org's has 17, because Hebrew counts the title ('The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's') as 1:1. Sixteen verses map onto sixteen. This stray identity entry would put the Latin's first line on the Hebrew title.

Bel and the Dragon is one verse out for its entire length in Vulgate numbering, and the file contains the evidence against itself. It carries both 'DAN 13:65 -> BEL 1:1' and 'DAN 14:1 -> BEL 1:1'. Those are not two printings of one verse, which is what an earlier reading of this file assumed: they are two different verses. The Clementine's Daniel 13:65 is 'Et rex Astyages appositus est ad patres suos', which is Bel 1:1; its 14:1 is 'Erat autem Daniel conviva regis', which is Bel 1:2. The Clementine closes Susanna with the Astyages sentence rather than opening Bel with it, so everything after is displaced by one. Measured against the Douay-Rheims, which translates the Clementine: Bel 1:n+1 beats Bel 1:n on 41 of the 42 verses of Daniel 14, the exception being 14:42, a sentence the Vulgate has and the Greek does not. Replaced below by the shifted range.

The *English* Jonah mapping, copied into the Vulgate file where it does not belong, and the proof is in the file's own maxVerses: it gives Vulgate Jonah chapter 1 sixteen verses, so the source verse 'JON 1:17' does not exist. Only the English tradition ends Jonah 1 at a seventeenth verse and puts the great fish there; the Vulgate follows the Hebrew, where the fish opens chapter 2. All four witnesses agree -- the Clementine and the Nova Vulgata both read 'Et praeparavit Dominus piscem grandem' at 2:1, the Douay-Rheims has no 1:17 at all and puts the fish at 2:1, and Brenton's Septuagint does the same; only the World English Bible has it at 1:17. With these two entries present every Vulgate citation of Jonah 2 resolved one verse late, so 'Jonah 2:1' returned Jonah's prayer instead of the fish that swallowed him. Dropped, leaving Jonah to map identically as it already does in org and lxx. Found by the textual alignment audit, which scored the mapped position at 0.28 against 1.00 one verse earlier.

Sends Vulgate Isaiah 8:22 to Hebrew 8:23, which is already claimed -- correctly -- by 'ISA 9:1 -> ISA 8:23'. The Vulgate's Isaiah 8 has 22 verses to the Hebrew's 23 precisely because the Hebrew's 8:23 ('At the first time the land of Zabulon...') opens the Vulgate's chapter 9. With this entry present, Hebrew 8:22 has no Latin source at all and 8:23 has two.

Both contradict 'ISA 9:2-21 -> ISA 9:1-20', which is exact and complete: the Vulgate's Isaiah 9 has 21 verses to org's 20 because Vulgate 9:1 is Hebrew 8:23 (stated by this file's own 'ISA 9:1 -> ISA 8:23'), leaving 9:2-21 to cover 9:1-20 twenty-for-twenty.

Upstream's fine-grained alignment of Greek Daniel 3 against the Song of the Three is internally inconsistent: 'DAG 3:52-23' is a malformed range (a transposed '3:52-53'), and DAG 3:52 is assigned to both S3Y 1:29 (via the 3:24-52 range) and S3Y 1:30. Replaced below by the coarse alignment, which is exact and independently checkable.

The Daniel 5/6 boundary, left untreated for Greek Daniel in the one file that also states it correctly for Hebrew Daniel. 'DAG 5:1-31 -> DAN 5:1-31' targets a verse org does not have, since org's Daniel 5 has thirty; and 'DAG 6:1-28 -> DAN 6:1-28' then leaves org's Daniel 6:29 unreachable. The sentence at issue is 'And Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom', which the Greek and Latin print as 5:31 and the Aramaic as 6:1 -- the Douay-Rheims and the World English Bible both put it at 5:31, and this same file already records the shift correctly for the ordinary Daniel: 'DAN 5:31 -> DAN 6:1' and 'DAN 6:1-28 -> DAN 6:2-29'. Replaced below with those three entries transposed onto DAG, which is the same correction lxx received.

rsc.reason: See _psalm_9_note. The Russian Synodal psalter follows the Greek numbering and carries the same two stray superscription entries as lxx and vul, verbatim: 'PSA 9:22 -> PSA 10:0' alongside the correct 'PSA 9:22-39 -> PSA 10:1-18', and 'PSA 113:9 -> PSA 115:0' alongside 'PSA 113:9-26 -> PSA 115:1-18'. Neither Hebrew psalm has a superscription for the stray entry to land on. Until this was applied, rsc could not be loaded at all -- Versification.load raised on the contradiction -- which went unnoticed because rsc is not in DEFAULT_SYSTEMS and so is never loaded unless asked for by name.

See _synodal_psalm_note. Contradicts the neighbouring 'PSA 86:2-7 -> PSA 87:2-7', which is exact and complete: Synodal Psalm 86 has 7 verses and org's 87 has 7, so 2-7 covers 2-7 six for six. This stray singleton additionally sends 86:2 to 87:1, which 'PSA 86:0-1 -> PSA 87:0-1' has already accounted for. Dropping it leaves the two surviving entries covering 0-7 exactly, which is what lxx and vul state in one range.

See _synodal_psalm_note. These three are mutually inconsistent and cannot all be right: 'PSA 89:0-1 -> PSA 90:0' maps two verses onto one, 'PSA 89:2-6 -> PSA 90:1-5' then shifts the psalm by one, and 'PSA 89:6 -> PSA 90:6' silently shifts it back so that the surviving 'PSA 89:7-17 -> PSA 90:7-17' lines up again. Synodal Psalm 89 and org Psalm 90 both have 17 verses and no verse is added or dropped between them, so the alignment is straight through -- exactly as lxx and vul both record it, in a single 'PSA 89:0-17 -> PSA 90:0-17'. Replaced below by the missing head of that range.

See _synodal_psalm_note. 'PSA 141:0 -> PSA 142:0-1' maps one verse onto two. The surviving 'PSA 141:1-7 -> PSA 142:2-8' is exact, leaving the Synodal's unnumbered title to correspond to org's title alone. Replaced below by the title-to-title mapping, which is what the rso file already states for this psalm.

rso.reason: See _psalm_9_note and the rsc entry above. The Catholic and Orthodox Russian Synodal files carry identical psalm mappings and identical faults.

See _synodal_psalm_note. 'PSA 86:0-1 -> PSA 87:1' maps two verses onto one, and 'PSA 86:2 -> PSA 87:1' claims the same target a third time while contradicting the exact 'PSA 86:2-7 -> PSA 87:2-7'. Both are replaced below by the head of the range, giving the straight-through alignment lxx, vul and the corrected rsc all agree on.

See _synodal_psalm_note. 'PSA 89:2-6 -> PSA 90:1-6' maps five verses onto six, and overlaps 'PSA 89:0-1 -> PSA 90:0-1', which has already accounted for org 90:1. Synodal Psalm 89 and org Psalm 90 both have 17 verses with nothing added or dropped between them, so 2-6 corresponds to 2-6; the surviving 'PSA 89:7-17 -> PSA 90:7-17' resumes exactly there.

See _synodal_psalm_note. Contradicts the tail of 'PSA 114:0-8 -> PSA 116:0-8', which is exact and complete for a psalm rso's own maxVerses gives 8 verses. The stray additionally sends 114:8 to org 116:9, apparently to express that one Orthodox verse covers two Hebrew ones -- a split no range can state, since both sides must be the same length. Dropping it leaves org 116:9 with no rso source, which is an honest gap rather than a verse claimed twice. The Catholic file does not have this problem: rsc gives its Psalm 114 nine verses and maps 0-9 to 116:0-9 straight through.

Two self-referential entries, '2ES 10:59 -> 2ES 10:59' and '2ES 10:60 -> 2ES 10:59', that contradict the twelve-chapter series around them. rso maps its 2 Esdras 3-14 onto org's EZA (4 Ezra) 1-12, chapter for chapter, and '2ES 10:1-60 -> EZA 8:1-60' covers this chapter exactly, sixty verses onto sixty. The strays would additionally send 2 Esdras 10:59 to itself and 10:60 back to 10:59, which is both a contradiction and, in the second case, off by one against a range that is already complete.

DAG 1:1-21.reason: See _dag_note. Identical to lxx's entry; the Greek and English number Daniel 1 alike.

DAG 3:1-23.reason: See _dag_note. Chapter 3 up to the point where the Song of the Three is inserted.

DAG 3:91-97.reason: See _dag_note. After the Song, Greek Daniel 3:91-97 resumes the Aramaic text at 3:24. Seven verses both sides.

DAG 4:1-3.reason: See _dag_note. Nebuchadnezzar's proclamation closes chapter 3 in the Aramaic and opens chapter 4 in the Greek.

DAG 4:4-37.reason: See _dag_note. The remainder of the chapter, thirty-four verses both sides.

DAG 5:1-30.reason: See _dag_note. Belshazzar's feast, identical up to his death at verse 30.

DAG 5:31.reason: 'And Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.' The English tradition prints it as the last verse of chapter 5 and org opens chapter 6 with it, which is why eng DAG 5 has 31 verses where lxx has 30. Without this the verse resolved into a nonexistent org DAG.

DAG 6:1-28.reason: The consequence of the verse above: all twenty-eight verses of the English chapter 6 run one behind org, which has twenty-nine. Confirmed on web against brenton -- 'It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom one hundred twenty local governors' is the Greek's 6:2, not its 6:1. Every verse of the lions' den was resolving one early, including 6:22, 'My God has sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths'.

DAG 7:1-28.reason: See _dag_note. From chapter 7 the two number alike again.

DAG 3:24-90.reason: English Bibles that print the Greek Daniel carry the Song of the Three inside chapter 3, exactly as the Vulgate and the Septuagint do, but upstream records the correspondence only for those two. Without it, a citation of the Song cannot reach an English text that has it. Both sides are 67 verses (90-24+1, and org gives S3Y 67), matching the entries this file's siblings state for lxx and vul. This replaces the broken S3Y-to-DAG chain dropped above, in the direction that is actually well-defined.

ISA 64:1.reason: Missing upstream, leaving English Isaiah 64:1 to fall through to Hebrew 64:1 and collide with English 64:2. English Isaiah 64 has 12 verses to the Hebrew's 11, and upstream's own 'ISA 64:2-12 -> ISA 64:1-11' already accounts for all eleven, leaving 64:1 with nowhere to go inside the chapter. It belongs to Hebrew 63:19: 'Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down' is the second half of the Hebrew's last verse of chapter 63. vul.json carries exactly this entry.

BAR 3:35-37.reason: Missing entirely, so the last three verses of Baruch 3 resolved one verse early from English numbering. The English tradition gives Baruch 3 thirty-seven verses where org, lxx, vul and nvl all give thirty-eight, because it merges the two halves of the star passage into a single 3:34 -- the World English Bible reads 'The stars shone in their watches, and were glad. When he called them, they said, Here we are', where the Douay-Rheims keeps 'and rejoiced' at 3:34 and 'They were called, and they said: Here we are' at 3:35. Everything after is displaced. Without this, a citation of Baruch 3:36 in English numbering returned 'He found out all the way of knowledge' instead of 'This is our God, and there shall no other be accounted of in comparison to him' -- a verse the tradition reads christologically, and one of the more likely in the book to be cited.

BAR 6:2-73.reason: Seventy-two verses onto seventy-two, leaving the English heading at 6:1 without an org counterpart because org does not number it. Brings the English into line with vul, which already states 'BAR 6:1-72 -> LJE 1:1-72' correctly, and with lxx and org, which both declare 72.

BAR 6:1.reason: The letter's heading, which org does not number separately. Without an entry it falls through to identity and lands on org BAR 6:1 -- a chapter org does not have, since its Baruch stops at five. Sent to the letter's first verse instead, which is where the heading belongs and what the previous whole-book range effectively did.

LJE 1:2-73.reason: Seventy-two onto seventy-two. Without it the last verse resolved to LJE 1:73, which org does not have. eng records this book twice, as Baruch 6 and as a standalone LJE, and only the Baruch 6 form had been corrected; this brings the two into agreement.

SIR 14:17.reason: The Latin splits the Greek's Sirach 14:16 in two, exactly as it does 6:19. latvuc 14:16 is 'Da et accipe, et justifica animam tuam' and 14:17 'Ante obitum tuum operare justitiam, quoniam non est apud inferos invenire cibum'; together they are org's single 14:16, 'Give, take, and treat yourself well, because there is no seeking of luxury in Hades'. Both number the chapter at 27 verses, so nothing counting can do would find this. Which side deviates was settled the same way as for chapter 6: eng agrees with lxx verse for verse across the whole chapter, so only vul moves.

SIR 14:18-25.reason: The eight verses carried by the split above. 'All flesh shall fade as grass' is the Vulgate's 14:18 and org's 14:17; 'He who looketh in at her windows, and hearkeneth at her door' is 14:24 against 14:23. They realign at 14:26 because the Vulgate's 14:25 runs org's 14:24 and 14:25 together, which is what absorbs the shift and why both chapters end at 27.

NEH 7:44.reason: The Clementine splits the Levites entry and nothing recorded it, so four verses of the list resolved one late. latvuc 7:43 is 'filii Josue et Cedmihel filiorum' and 7:44 is 'Oduiae, septuaginta quatuor. Cantores:' -- together the Nova Vulgata's single 7:43, 'Levitae: filii Iesua, hi sunt filii Cadmihel, Bennui et Odoviae, septuaginta quattuor'. Confirmed twice over: Latin against Latin, and web against the Douay-Rheims, which puts 'The singers: the children of Asaph: one hundred forty-eight' at English 7:44 and Vulgate 7:45.

NEH 7:45-47.reason: The three verses carried by the split above -- singers, gatekeepers, temple servants. They resynchronise at 7:48, which the Clementine runs together where the Nova Vulgata has 7:47 and 7:48 separately ('filii Ceros, filii Siaa, filii Phadon, filii Lebana, filii Hagaba' against those five names split across two verses). Nothing is claimed here about 7:67-73: the Nova Vulgata's own tail disagrees with org there -- its 7:72 is 'Et quod dedit reliquus populus' where the Leningrad Codex has the priests dwelling in their cities -- so the Latin witnesses cannot settle that region and the vendored mapping is left as it stands.

SIR 6:20.reason: The Latin splits the Greek's Sirach 6:19 in two and nothing recorded it, so fifteen verses of the chapter resolved one early. latvuc 6:19 is 'Quasi is qui arat et seminat accede ad eam, et sustine bonos fructus illius' and 6:20 is 'In opere enim ipsius exiguum laborabis, et cito edes de generationibus illius' -- together they are org's single 6:19, 'Come to her as one who plows and sows and wait for her good fruit; for your toil shall be little'. The Douay-Rheims splits it identically, so this is the Vulgate tradition rather than one edition's quirk. Which side was wrong was settled by triangulation: eng and lxx agree with org verse for verse across the whole chapter, so only vul deviates.

SIR 6:21-35.reason: The consequence of the split above: fifteen verses, one behind for their whole length. 'Give ear, my son, and take wise counsel' is the Vulgate's 6:24 and org's 6:23; 'Put thy feet into her fetters' is 6:25 against 6:24. They realign at 6:36 because the Vulgate has no counterpart to org 6:35, 'Be willing to listen to every godly discourse' -- which is why both number the chapter at 37 despite the split.

PSA 12:0.reason: Restores the title-to-title link dropped with 'PSA 12:0-1'. The Vulgate prints Psalm 12's superscription unnumbered (verse 0); Hebrew Psalm 13 counts it as verse 1.

DAG 3:24-90.reason: Greek Daniel 3:24-90 is the Song of the Three, which org carries as the standalone book S3Y. Both sides are 67 verses (90-24+1 = 67, and org maxVerses S3Y = 67), so the alignment is one-to-one and in order. Matches the well-formed 'DAN 3:24-90 -> S3Y 1:1-67' already present in this same file for the Vulgate's Daniel.

DAN 14:1-41.reason: Replaces the two dropped entries. The Clementine puts the opening of Bel and the Dragon at the end of Susanna (13:65 -> BEL 1:1, which upstream already has and which is correct), so its chapter 14 begins at the Greek's second verse and runs one behind for the whole book. Forty-one verses onto forty-one. Daniel 14:42, 'Tunc rex ait: Paveant omnes habitantes in universa terra Deum Danielis', has no Greek counterpart and is deliberately left unmapped rather than forced onto a verse that does not exist.

DAG 5:1-30.reason: Thirty verses onto thirty, up to the point where the traditions part.

DAG 5:31.reason: 'And Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom': the last verse of chapter 5 in the Greek and Latin, the first of chapter 6 in the Aramaic.

DAG 6:1-28.reason: The remainder of the chapter, displaced by one, exactly as the file's own 'DAN 6:1-28 -> DAN 6:2-29' already states for Hebrew Daniel.

DEU 29:1.reason: See fix_max_verses.lxx.DEU. Copied from eng's and vul's identical entries.

DEU 29:2-29.reason: See fix_max_verses.lxx.DEU. The other 28 verses of the chapter.

1KI 20:1-29.reason: Greek 3 Kingdoms swaps the Naboth and Ben-Hadad chapters, and upstream records only half the swap. '1KI 21:1-43 -> 1KI 20:1-43' is there and correct; its partner is missing, so all 29 verses of Greek chapter 20 fell through to the identity and every citation of them returned Ben-Hadad's siege where Naboth's vineyard belongs. The verse counts prove the swap on their own -- lxx 20 has 29 verses against org 21's 29, and lxx 21 has 43 against org 20's 43 -- and the text confirms it at both ends and the middle: Brenton's 20:1 'And Nabuthai the Jezraelite had a vineyard' is org's 21:1 'Navot the Yizre'eli', his 20:15 'when Jezabel heard it' is org's 21:15 'when Izevel heard that Navot was stoned', and his 20:29 'how Achaab has been pricked to the heart' is org's 21:29 'how Ach'av humbleth himself'. The Vulgate follows the Hebrew order throughout and agrees with org.

NUM 27:4-7.reason: The Septuagint has no counterpart to org's Numbers 27:4, the daughters' plea 'Why should the name of our father be withdrawn from among his family, because he has no son?', so four verses run one behind. Brenton's 27:4 is 'And Moses brought their case before the Lord', which is org 27:5; his 27:6 'The daughters of Salpaad have spoken rightly' is org 27:7. They resynchronise at 27:9 because the Greek splits org 27:8, keeping 'And thou shalt speak to the children of Israel, saying' apart from 'If a man die, and have no son'. Equal counts, different division -- the same shape as the Leviticus 8 omission recorded above, and equally invisible to any count-based check.

EZK 7:3-6.reason: Greek Ezekiel 7 transposes two blocks of the oracle and nothing recorded it, so seven verses resolved into the wrong half of the chapter. The Greek runs the Hebrew's 6,7,8,9 first and then its 3,4,5. Brenton's 7:3 'The end is come' is org 7:6 'Ketz is come, the ketz is come'; his 7:5 'Now I will pour out mine anger upon thee' is org 7:8 'Now will I shortly pour out My fury upon thee'. Four verses onto four. The alignment that found this could not describe it -- a monotonic alignment cannot express a swap, so it reported a plain one-verse shift over part of the block; the correspondence here was established by reading the two texts.

EZK 7:7-9.reason: The other half of the transposition above. Brenton's 7:7 'Now the end is come to thee, and I will send judgment upon thee' is org 7:3 'Now is the Ketz come upon thee, and I will send Mine anger'; his 7:9 'For thus saith the Lord; Behold, the end is come' is org 7:5 'Thus saith Adonoi Hashem; A ra'ah, a singular ra'ah, hinei, has come'. Three onto three, and the chapter resynchronises at 7:10, which is why both number it at 27 and no count-based check could see any of this.

LEV 8:19-29.reason: The Septuagint has no counterpart to org's Leviticus 8:19, 'He killed it; and Moses sprinkled the blood around on the altar', so eleven verses of the consecration run one behind and nothing recorded it. Brenton's 8:19 is 'And he divided the ram by its limbs', which is org's 8:20; 'And Moses took the breast, and separated it for a heave-offering' is his 8:28 against org's 8:29. They resynchronise at 8:31 because the Greek splits org's 8:30 in two, keeping 'And he sanctified Aaron and his garments' as its own 8:30 -- which is why both number the chapter at 36 despite the omission, and why no count-based check could see it. Three independent pairs flagged the run (lxx against vul 10-0, eng against lxx 8-0, org against lxx 8-0) and eng agrees with org here verse for verse across the whole chapter, so only lxx deviates.

DAG 3:24-90.reason: Upstream lxx.json maps DAG 3:1-23 and DAG 3:91-97 but leaves 3:24-90 unmapped, so citing the Song of the Three against a Septuagint corpus silently resolved to nothing. lxx maxVerses DAG chapter 3 is 97, leaving exactly verses 24-90 (67 verses) for the Song, matching org's S3Y of 67 verses.

Brenton and Swete both print Deuteronomy 28 with 68 verses and 29 with 29, exactly as the World English Bible does, while lxx declared 69 and 28 as org and the Nova Vulgata do. eng and vul each carry the pair of mappings this needs and lxx carried none, so all 29 verses of Greek Deuteronomy 29 resolved one out -- including 29:29 'The secret things belong to the Lord our God'. DAN.reason: The Clementine's Daniel 14 has 42 verses and vul declared 41, so its last verse -- 'Then the king said: Let all the inhabitants of the whole earth fear the God of Daniel' -- could not be cited, validated or rendered at all. Both Vulgate witnesses print it. It has no Greek counterpart: Bel ends at 42 and the Latin runs one ahead throughout because the Clementine prints the Astyages verse as Daniel 13:65, so 'DAN 14:1-41 -> BEL 1:2-42' is complete and 14:42 is a Latin plus. Conversion of it still refuses, which is right; what changes is that the verse now exists.

vul.reason: The Vulgate versification defines Daniel twice: DAN, the Vulgate's own 14-chapter Daniel, and DAG, Greek Daniel. Both map onto the same org verses, so converting org->vul has two candidate answers for all of Daniel, Susanna, Bel and the Song of the Three. Without a preference the tie-break falls to whichever book code sorts first, which is DAG -- meaning a citation rendered against a Douay-Rheims text would come back in Greek Daniel's numbering. DAN is what a Vulgate or Douay-Rheims corpus actually prints, so DAG is only chosen when nothing else maps.

eng.reason: The English versification defines the Letter of Jeremiah twice: as Baruch chapter 6, which is how English Bibles actually print it, and as a standalone LJE. Both map onto the same org verses, so converting org->eng has two candidate answers for the whole letter, and without a preference the tie-break falls to whichever book code sorts first -- which is LJE, the form no English Bible uses. The corpora settle it: the World English Bible and the Douay-Rheims both print Baruch 6 and neither has a standalone book, so a citation resolved into eng should say Baruch 6. DAG is here for the same reason and was added with the Greek Daniel mappings: English versification defines Daniel twice as well, as DAN and as Greek Daniel DAG, and once DAG maps onto org's DAN the reverse lookup has two answers for the whole book. DAG sorts first, so without this an ordinary citation of Daniel 4 came back in Greek Daniel's numbering and no English protocanon corpus could render it. DAN is what an English Bible prints unless it is specifically a Greek Daniel, so DAG is chosen only when nothing else maps.

org.reason: org.json's mappedVerses do not map another versification onto org -- they record where the standalone book S3Y sits inside Greek Daniel, an aside rather than a conversion. They are also inconsistent with org's own maxVerses (the final range 'S3Y 1:38-68 -> DAG 3:60-90' cites S3Y verse 68, but org maxVerses gives S3Y only 67 verses). Since org is the pivot, org-to-org conversion is the identity and these entries are not needed.

unreliable.reason: Esther's Greek additions cannot be resolved from the upstream data. org.json gives ESG the verse counts ['39','23','22','47','28','14','10','39','32','13'] -- byte-identical to eng.json's -- while its mappings target subverse refs (ESG 1:1a ... 1:1s, 4:17a ... 4:17z) that do not fit that grid. Chapter 4 is the clearest case: eng verses 4:18-47 collapse onto 24 distinct org subverses, giving org 41 units where maxVerses claims 47. The additions are also many-to-one in places (eng ESG 4:20 and 4:21 both map to org ESG 4:17c), so the mapping is not invertible. Superseded by esther_clementine.json, which is built against the Swete and Douay-Rheims texts and hand-checked; until that table is in place, citing ESG raises rather than guessing.

The Vulgate's Esther cannot be lined up with the original-language numbering verse by verse. Chapters 1:1-10:3 correspond straightforwardly, but 10:4-16:24 are the six Greek additions, which the Septuagint interleaves through the book rather than appending -- Addition B sits inside chapter 3, Addition C inside chapter 4, Addition D inside chapter 5 -- and the upstream data for that interleaving is the self-contradictory ESG material rejected above. The correspondence that can be established, and is, is between Vulgate numbering and the A-F letter chapters; see esther_additions.json. Cite Esther's additions in Vulgate or letter numbering and quote them from the Douay-Rheims.

Jerome translated Judith and Tobit from Aramaic recensions differing from the Greek by whole clauses, and the automatic guard only refuses a chapter whose verse count differs from the pivot's -- so the handful whose counts coincide converted by identity and returned a plausible verse containing different words. Two of Judith's sixteen chapters did that and one of Tobit's fourteen, which is the worst of both: most of the book refuses and a few chapters quietly lie. Judith 6 is the proof that the coincidence means nothing -- both number the chapter at 21 verses, and the Douay's 6:9 'they tied Achior to a tree' is the Greek's 6:13 'bound Achior, cast him down, left him at the foot of the hill', four verses apart. Measured before deciding: aligning the Douay against the World English Bible across the whole of Judith scores 0.289, barely over the floor where an ordinary book runs 0.6 to 0.8; 72 of some 345 verses have no counterpart on the other side at all; and the offsets scatter *within* almost every chapter -- seven distinct ones across the 21 matched verses of chapter 7, eight across the 24 of chapter 13. That is a different text rather than a differently numbered one, and no mapping can express it. Confined to vul deliberately. The Nova Vulgata went back to the Greek for Judith and its verse counts are identical to org's, so eng, lxx, org and nvl line up with each other and only Jerome's own numbering stands apart. Sirach is left out for the opposite reason: it is partly mappable, and Sirach 6 is now mapped.

Sirach 18 is unmappable and both traditions number it at 33 verses, so the automatic guard cannot see it and it converted by identity. Read against the Greek, the Vulgate merges, expands, omits and splits inside fourteen verses: its 18:1 runs org's 18:1 and 18:2 together ('He that liveth for ever created all things together. God only shall be justified'), its 18:2 and 18:3 expand org's single 18:4, it has no counterpart to org 18:10 'As a drop of water from the sea, and a pebble from the sand', and its 18:10-11 and 18:12-13 each split one verse of org's. Five structural differences in both directions, which is the signature that made Jerome's Judith unmappable, in miniature. Chapters 6 and 14 of the same book are mapped, which is why this is a chapter rather than the book: the Vulgate's Sirach follows the Greek in most places and departs from it in a few, and refusing the whole book would throw away two verified fixes.
